title: TracePlayground long-tail anatomy notes
content:
Purpose
----
Quick working notes from TracePlayground replay sessions focused on the long-tail (p95/p99) behavior for the last two weeks of traffic. Goal: identify recurring stage-level hotspots that disproportionately impact p99 and produce an actionable experiment list (small, medium, gated).

Context / why this matters
- p50 and p95 are stable under current batching heuristics, but p99 has been drifting up ~20% over the past month on customer heavy-seq workloads.
- Long-tail requests are where customers notice flakiness and where SLAs are most at risk.
- TracePlayground lets us replay real traces with controlled variants (cold cache, different batch sizes, forced preemption) and profile runtime stages.

High-level findings (replay summary)
- Dataset: sample of 120k traces from production (sample window: 2024-10-20 -> 2024-11-03). Selected cohort: seq_len > 600 or with >1 tool call.
- Baseline metrics (TracePlayground default config): p50=180ms, p95=420ms, p99=980ms.
- p99 is dominated by three stage patterns: 1) KV cache miss + cold-kv fetch + compiler rewarm (~34%), 2) Large-batch contention / scheduling jitter (~27%), 3) Egress/transport spikes due to chunked streaming serialization (~18%). Remaining ~21% is noise (hardware preemptions, unexpected GC).

Representative per-stage breakdown (median of top-10 p99 traces)
- Tokenize: 8ms (median), 12ms (p95)
- Encode/embedding preproc: 18ms, 32ms
- KV lookup (cache hit): 6ms; KV lookup (miss + fetch): 210ms (observed outliers to 520ms)
- Model forward (gen): 340ms (variable by batch size)
- KV stitch/writeback: 28ms (miss cases add 150ms)
- Emitter/serializer (streaming): 54ms (spikes when chunk count > 8)
- Network egress: 120ms (p99 spikes correlated with client-side backpressure)

Notes on KV cache pathology
- Pattern: a multi-seq request where prefix tokens exceed cached KV capacity; first token batches trigger an async fetch to remote store (S3-like) and stalls model emit while waiting for KV materialization.
- Replays show fetch latency is bimodal: ~30–90ms for synchronous warm paths and ~200–600ms when cold (cold paths coincide with cache eviction window events around 4h mark).
- Hypothesis: our cache eviction policy is too aggressive for frequent long sequences on low-traffic users — causing expensive cold fetches during bursts.
- Quick experiments to run: increase per-shard cache budget by 20% (temporary), enable prefetching on sequences predicted to exceed a threshold, and measure p99 improvement.

Batcher contention observations
- Under heavy-replay (simulating a spike), batches occasionally exceed the configured max_batch_size due to concurrent queue draining plus async handoffs. The scheduling jitter correlates with host-level CPU steal and RX queue spikes.
- When batch sizes grow >6 (our baseline), model forward latency per token increases superlinearly because of workspace mem contention and kernel-launch queuing on older CUDA drivers.
- Mitigation arms: cap effective concurrent batchers per-GPU, add jittered enqueue delays to avoid stomp storms, and test newer driver/kernels in canary.

Emitter/streaming serialization causes
- Long responses that use chunked streaming see per-chunk serialization overhead (protobuf -> netbuf) that stacks up when emitter threads are saturated.
- Two operational knobs: increase emitter thread pool for high-output routes, or use a zero-copy serializer path for chunked streaming (experimental branch exists in PR#83).

TracePlayground replay configuration (how I ran experiments)
- Repository: github.com/redwood-inference/traceplayground (replay harness).
- Command: ./replay --input traces/longtail-sample-20241101.ndjson --cfg replay-configs/production-like.json --inject-cold-kv 0.12 --max-concurrency 48 --batcher-policy adaptive
- Important flags used: --inject-cold-kv (force fraction of traces to simulate cold cache), --collect-stages (per-token stage timestamps), --preserve-arrival (honor original inter-arrival times to surface queueing effects).
- Note: to reproduce exact p99 numbers seed RNG with --seed 4321 (we saw small variance across seeds).

Actionable experiment plan (priority ordered)
- Fast wins (<2 days, low-risk):
  1) Increase emitter thread pool to 32 for high-output routes and replay. Measure streaming serialization p99. (Owner: Evan)
  2) Add a short randomized enqueue jitter (2–6ms) in batching path to reduce simultaneous wake storms. (Owner: Sofia)
- Medium (1–2 weeks):
  3) Prefetch KV for traces where prefix length > 400 tokens (heuristic). Add feature flag and AB test. (Owner: Priya)
  4) Cap max concurrent batches per-GPU to 6 and run throughput/latency tradeoff sweep. (Owner: Tomás)
- Gated / requires infra & SRE signoff (2–6 weeks):
  5) Experiment with less aggressive shard-level eviction (increase per-shard reserved bytes by 20%). Monitor memory pressure and do canary rollout. (Owner: Platform Eng)
  6) Deploy zero-copy serializer for chunked streaming in a canary region. (Owner: DevExp + Observability)

Open questions / unknowns
- Are remote KV fetch spikes correlated with S3 regional IO throttling? Need to pull metrics from infra (S3 tail latencies) and correlate timestamps — linked_artifacts has a Confluence runbook that explains traces mapping.
- Some p99 traces show >2s model forward spikes even with small batches — could be driver/kernel pathologies on older GPU hosts. Need to identify host IDs from trace metadata and map to hw image/driver versions.

Next steps (for this doc)
- Run the two fast-win experiments in TracePlayground and attach raw replay run logs to this doc.
- Create a small dashboard: p99 contribution by stage (stacked bar), top offender traces list (with raw trace IDs) and host/driver mapping. Ask Observability for a temporary dashboard slot.
- Post a short summary to #runtime-latency with TL;DR and a link to the follow-up runbook.

Notes to self (fragments / checklist)
- Grab host mapping for replay run id rp-20241128-17: we saw 14/120k traces on those hosts.
- Re-run replay with --max-concurrency 24 and 72 to check non-linear effects.
- Check PR#83 zero-copy patch — maybe test locally with smaller streaming payloads first.
- Slack thread: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C03UJ2XKQ/p2024-11-29T13:04:10 (discussion with Tomás about cap heuristics).

Appendix: sample trace excerpt (token timestamps, ms)
- trace_id: rp-20241101-0002
  arrival: 2024-10-30T12:03:14.231Z
  steps: tokenize(6) -> kv-lookup(start:12,end:14,hit) -> forward(start:15,end:360) -> emit-chunk(361) -> serialize(420) -> egress(450)
- long-tail example:
  trace_id: rp-20241101-0921
  arrival: 2024-10-30T18:19:03.124Z
  steps: tokenize(10) -> kv-lookup(start:20,end:25,miss->fetch-start:26,fetch-end:310) -> forward(start:311,end:960) -> kv-stitch(980) -> emit(1010) -> serialize(1068) -> egress(1302)

If anything here is unclear or you want the raw replay logs attached to the doc, say so and I'll upload the zipped run outputs and the small script used to extract per-stage deltas.

-- Priya
